summary.title: Two Generals' Problem - Wikipedia
summary.one_liner: Two armies can never be certain they will attack simultaneously when they coordinate only over an unreliable messenger link, because no finite protocol guarantees both sides know the other has agreed.
takeaways: Two parties communicating over a lossy link cannot guarantee agreement, since every acknowledgement can also be lost and an infinite chain of confirmations would be needed.
The impossibility proof shows that any fixed deterministic protocol, and any non-deterministic one, fails: the last delivered message leaves one general attacking while the other does not.
Practical systems mitigate the problem by accepting uncertainty, e.g. sending many messengers, streaming acknowledgements, or numbering messages to estimate channel reliability.
The problem underlies the Byzantine Generals problem and explains why TCP cannot guarantee state consistency between endpoints.
The impossibility result was first published by Akkoyunlu, Ekanadham and Huber in 1975 and named by Jim Gray in 1978.
summary.summary: This Wikipedia article describes the Two Generals' Problem, a thought experiment in computing about coordinating an attack by messenger over an unreliable link. It walks through the intuitive failure of adding acknowledgements, then gives a proof sketch for deterministic protocols and an argument extending it to non-deterministic ones. It also covers engineering mitigations such as sending many messengers or using silence as a signal, and the history of the result from the 1975 paper to Jim Gray's 1978 naming.
